lesson.title: Protons, Neutrons, and Electrons: The Three Particles That Build Every Atom
lesson.summary: All atoms are built from just three subatomic particles, protons, neutrons, and electrons, whose distinct charges, masses, and locations explain why atoms have the structure that Rutherford's and Thomson's experiments first revealed.
lesson.body:
The historical sequence of atomic models, from Dalton's solid sphere through Thomson's plum pudding to Rutherford's nuclear atom, was really a sequence of discoveries about three subatomic particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons. Every atom of every element, from hydrogen to the heaviest synthetic elements, is built from some combination of these three particles, the true foundation of atomic structure. Each particle is defined by three properties, its electric charge, its mass, and its location within the atom, and those properties explain essentially everything Rutherford's gold foil experiment revealed about atomic structure.

The proton carries a positive charge, assigned a relative value of positive 1, and has a mass of approximately 1.673 x 10^-27 kg, simplified to about 1 atomic mass unit, or 1 amu. Protons reside in the atom's nucleus, the small, dense core Rutherford's experiment revealed when alpha particles bounced back from the gold foil rather than passing through. The number of protons in a nucleus is the atomic number, and this number defines which element an atom is: every atom with exactly 1 proton is hydrogen, every atom with exactly 6 protons is carbon, and every atom with exactly 79 protons is gold, regardless of how many neutrons or electrons it has.

The neutron, discovered later than the proton, carries no electric charge, reflected directly in its name, and has a mass of approximately 1.675 x 10^-27 kg, almost identical to the proton's and also simplified to about 1 amu. Neutrons also reside in the nucleus, packed together with the protons, and neutrons, along with the strong nuclear force, help hold the nucleus together despite the mutual repulsion between the positively charged protons packed at such short range. Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons, called isotopes, which share identical chemical behavior but differ in mass and sometimes stability, as with radioactive carbon 14 compared to stable carbon 12.

The electron carries a negative charge, a relative value of negative 1, exactly opposite the proton's, but its mass, about 9.109 x 10^-31 kg, is roughly 1836 times smaller than a proton's, essentially negligible for an atom's total mass. Electrons occupy the large volume of mostly empty space surrounding the nucleus, exactly the region most of Rutherford's alpha particles passed through undeflected, since electrons are too light to redirect a much heavier alpha particle. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so their opposite charges balance to zero net charge; an atom that has gained or lost electrons carries a net charge and is called an ion instead.

Putting these three particles together explains the structure every atomic model was ultimately trying to capture. A neutral carbon atom has 6 protons and 6 electrons, plus commonly 6 neutrons in its most abundant isotope, carbon 12. The 6 protons and 6 neutrons, each contributing about 1 amu, account for nearly all of the atom's mass, roughly 12 amu total, packed into the tiny nuclear volume, while the 6 electrons, contributing almost no mass, occupy a region tens of thousands of times larger in diameter. This is precisely why chemical reactions, which involve atoms exchanging or sharing electrons, do not change an atom's mass in any meaningful way, and why the nucleus, protected deep inside that far larger electron cloud, stays essentially untouched during ordinary bonding, a distinction essential once you start studying how atoms bond to form molecules and compounds.
